23.0.0.en: Balaam asked Balak to build him seven altars on the high places of Baal, "here," and asked that a bull and a ram be sacrificed on each altar to offer to the Lord. We do not know why he asked for seven altars instead of one, but some see that he did so in honor of the Lord, who had not forgotten His angel with the drawn sword.

23.1.0.en: Because of Balak's confidence in Balaam and the power of his prophecy or the power of his sorcery, he responded at once and offered a bull and a ram on each altar, and Balak, as the priest for his people, took part in offering up these burnt offerings on the seven altars.

23.2.0.en: A bare height: a high place.

23.2.1.en: Balaam asked Balak to remain beside his altars and his sacrifices, while he would go alone to a high place, perhaps the Lord would answer and speak with him, and Balaam promised Balak that he would tell him all that the Lord said to him or showed him.

23.3.0.en: We do not know how the Lord came to Balaam, whether it was a vision or He sent him an angel, but we find Balaam speaking with God of all that he had done in building the altars and offering burnt offerings on them, and perhaps by this saying he wanted to appease God with these seven altars.

23.4.0.en: God spoke with Balaam and put a word in his mouth and commanded him to return to Balak and to speak this word. And indeed Balaam returned to Balak and found him standing by his altars and his burnt offerings, with the chiefs and great men of his people.

23.5.0.en: He took up his parable: the four discourses of Balaam were called parables, perhaps because of the wisdom they contain and because they were spoken in a measured prose form that approached poetry.

23.5.1.en: Aram: highlands between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates, that is, present-day Iraq.

23.5.2.en: Balaam said at the beginning of his discourse, "Balak the king of Moab hath brought me from Aram, out of the mountains of the east," saying, "Come, curse me Jacob, and come, defy Israel." It is to be noted in this that Balaam pronounced the old name Jacob and his new title Israel, which confirms that what he spoke was a spirit of prophecy from God.

23.6.0.en: Balaam rejects answering Balak's request and declares clearly that he cannot curse or revile what God has not cursed. He continues his discourse that he sees this people with its abundant number from his high place on which he stands, that is, "the top of the rocks," and describes the people of God as follows:

23.6.1.en: 1- A people dwelling alone: that is, it is an independent people that does not share with the pagan peoples in their evils or their pagan sacrifices, but has its own divine laws.

23.6.2.en: 2- Not reckoned among the nations: that is, God distinguished it from the rest of the peoples and considered it a chosen people and a firstborn son to Him.

23.6.3.en: The fourth part: a dwelling or tents.

23.7.0.en: Who can count this great people, in whose number God gave blessing so that it became like the sand of the earth and its dust (Gen 22:17), indeed who can even count the number of the tents of this people, as an allusion to the abundance of number and strength. And after Balaam uttered this speech that the Lord put in his mouth, he turned his speech to something else, for he wished for himself that his life on earth might end having received a blessing like that which God reserved for His people Israel, so that his soul would die like these righteous ones and he would have a share in the eternity that God prepared for them.

23.7.1.en: It is to be noted that this speech is the word of God on the tongue of Balaam and not the feelings of his heart, as is proved by the fact that he afterward devised a plot to destroy the children of Israel (ch. 25).

23.8.0.en: Balak was distressed by Balaam's words, so Balak reproached him, saying to him, I brought you and honored you to curse this people, and behold you bless them instead of cursing them. Balaam answered him that he had done nothing except utter what the Lord had declared to him, and he can do nothing else.

23.8.1.en: May your wishes for life with God become real action through earnest striving, and be confident that God will support you to enjoy fellowship with Him and then to rejoice in eternal life with Him.

23.9.0.en: The utmost part of them: its far extremities.

23.9.1.en: The field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah: the top of Pisgah is one of the peaks of the chain of mountains of Abarim that extends northeast of the Dead Sea, and the field of Zophim was on this peak, and from the top of Pisgah Moses saw the land of Canaan before he died (Deut 34:1) (map 6). Balak thought that when Balaam saw this people in its abundant number from his place, the high places of Baal, he was terrified by the greatness of the number and therefore did not curse the people, and so he invited him to accompany him to another place, also high, which is the top of one of the hills. Balak's aim in this new place was that Balaam should see only a part or an edge of the people, that is, a small part, so that his soul might be reassured and he could curse the people. And Balak did as Balaam had asked at first, for he built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.

23.10.0.en: These three verses are a similar repetition of what came in verses (3-5) of the same chapter.

23.11.0.en: After Balaam returned from his second retreat and Balak's anxious question about what the Lord had spoken with him, Balaam began to speak, addressing Balak, saying to him, rise up and listen well and prepare yourself for the word that God has sent you, for God is the God of truth and not like man, who is liable to lie, and not like the sons of men who issue judgments and then repent of them and withdraw what they have spoken. Is it reasonable that God should say something and not do it (God forbid), or give a promise and not be able to fulfill it?! For God has promised His people blessing, and He must fulfill His promise.

23.11.1.en: Sometimes it is mentioned in the Holy Bible that God repents of a decision He issued, as happened with the people of Nineveh in the days of Jonah, and what is meant is an expression that human beings understand, namely repentance, but the truth is that God is compassionate and forgives men if they repent; the change comes from men, and it is repentance, and so God forgives them.

23.12.0.en: I, Balaam, was commanded earlier and now by God to bless this people and not curse them, and God has indeed blessed this people, so who am I that I should oppose or annul His blessing?

23.13.0.en: The shout of a king: they used to sound trumpets at the feasts to glorify God their King.

23.13.1.en: We cannot forget the people's earlier errors and their murmurings and God's punishment of them, but with all this, God in His love and mercy sees no fault in His people so long as they repent and are sorry for their evil. Though He punishes them, He is a Father who pities the weaknesses of men. He called His people to come out of Egypt knowing all that would come from them, and He even declares that He saw in His people no fault or sin for which they deserve a curse, for the Lord their God is with them and dwells in their midst as their King, and they sing and praise His holy name.

23.13.2.en: And the people of God are distinguished from the rest of the Gentile peoples by their faith in God, and their errors toward God they quickly turn back from, so He means the relative perfection of His people.

23.14.0.en: The unicorn (reem): one of the swift kinds of gazelles (the antelope).

23.14.3.en: Balaam continues his discourse and says, is this not the people that its God brought out with the right hand of His power from the land of Egypt, and it went out of it with the speed of the gazelle and no harm from Pharaoh and his soldiers overtook it? Therefore nothing of the works of sorcerers will afflict this people, whether sorcery or astrology, for it is a people that shelters in its great God, and a time will come (after the people's settling) when it will be told among the nations what God has done with His people from their going out of Egypt until their victory over the nations and their possessing the land.

23.15.0.en: It is a people that rises to attack its enemies with the strength of the lioness (the female lion), which is famous for hunting, seizing prey and speed more than the male lions, and it lifts itself up among the nations like the lion, which has more authority than the rest of the animals, and God has given this people victory, for it does not rest nor sleep until it finishes off all its enemies among the nations and destroys them.

23.15.1.en: My beloved brother ... how beautiful is the heart of God, who forgives His people and does not forsake them before their enemies ... The prodigal son sinned, and yet his compassionate father received him on his return (Lk 15). So take courage, and encourage others also to repent, for Christ receives everyone in tenderness when they repent and confess, for He does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he return and live.. and He keeps His promises and covenants to all His people.

23.16.0.en: Balak was greatly distressed and enraged by Balaam's discourse, and therefore we find him asking Balaam that if he was not able to curse the people, then at least he should not bless them, but Balaam's answer to Balak came that he had already informed him that he would not speak anything of his own, but everything the Lord speaks he would tell to Balak.

23.17.0.en: In a new attempt and an unjustified insistence, Balak proposed to Balaam to take him to another place, in the hope that the Lord would change His mind and, with the new sacrifices, permit the cursing of His people.

23.17.1.en: In this third attempt of Balak we discover the stubbornness and stupidity of the wicked man in understanding God or His purposes. King Balak did not despair of trying to bribe God with sacrifices or to bribe Balaam himself, who in his third obedience to Balak also reveals the evil lust of his heart to obtain Balak's material blessings, as if God changes His mind, though he knew well that God is not a man that He should change His mind or turn back from what He promised (v. 19).

23.18.0.en: The top of Peor: one of the mountain peaks overlooking the wilderness, on which the pagan Baal "Peor" was worshiped, and it is the northern peak of the mountains of Abarim (map 6). Balak took Balaam to the holiest of the hills to him and his people, for they sacrifice there to the god "Peor," and he thought that this place had a special standing and an awesome holiness that might make God change His thought and heart if the burnt offerings were offered from this place... And this place was high, so it overlooks the whole wilderness in which Israel pitches its tents.

23.19.0.en: And as he had done before, Balaam asked that seven altars be built and burnt offerings be offered on them, consisting of seven bulls and seven rams. And Balak also did what Balaam asked of him, for he was thirsty to curse the people whatever the price or cost.

23.19.1.en: If God proclaims His voice to you to repent of your sins, return to Him and do not persist in your snare, taking advantage of God's longsuffering, for His mercy is upon you if you benefit from it, but your making light of His mercies will in the end bring His wrath upon you and you will perish.

23.19.2.en: The third and fourth discourses of Balaam

24.0.0.en: The wilderness: the wilderness of Moab adjoining the Dead Sea, in which the children of Israel pitched their tents, that is, Balaam looked toward the people of the children of Israel.

24.0.1.en: In the two previous times Balaam would leave the altars and go far away into retreat to receive the divine revelation, but this time, as he was sure that the Lord wanted to bless the people and not curse them, he thought it good to remain in his place, looking toward the wilderness toward the people and waiting for God's revelation to come upon him.

24.0.2.en: To meet with enchantments: that is, to receive a revelation or a divine message.

24.1.0.en: Balaam looked at the people abiding in the camp around the tent of meeting with all its twelve tribes, and the Spirit of God came upon him, so he prophesied and spoke before Balak that what he uttered was not his own word but a revelation from God, a revelation to a man whose eyes are open, that is, it was granted him by God to see and hear what God wanted to convey to Balak.

24.2.0.en: He declares and confirms again that he speaks what he hears from God, and that he sees a heavenly vision, majestic and fearful, that makes him fall to the ground in fear and reverence for it. The expression "having his eyes open" means that it is a true vision and not a dream about which people may differ.

24.3.0.en: Balaam uttered sweet words about the people of Israel, describing the beauty of its tents around the tent of meeting with its order and the banners of its tribes, and he also describes it as having an abundance of number extending like gardens and orchards and like the trees of lign aloes, fragrant, which God blessed and planted and tended, and its tents are also likened to the tall cedar trees, famous for the high price of their wood and their greenness throughout the year ... and all these similes point to the standing of this people in the heart of God.

24.4.0.en: His buckets: the plural of bucket, that is, a vessel with which they fill water.

24.4.1.en: Agag: a title that was given to the kings of the people of Amalek, as the title Pharaoh was given to the kings of Egypt.

24.4.2.en: Balaam continued describing the people and praising them, using poetry and symbol, and he says that this people in its descendants and multiplication will be like the water overflowing from a full bucket when it is carried, and he repeats the meaning again in a new form using the expression "many waters," while its kingdom will be a great and exalted kingdom, and its kings will be higher than the kings of the Amalekites, who bear the title Agag.

24.5.0.en: Break their bones: breaks and grinds the bones with his teeth.

24.5.1.en: His arrows: that is, the arrows of Agag, the strongest of the kings in the region.

24.5.2.en: God enveloped it in His love and care, so He brought it out with a strong arm from Egypt, and the people became like the gazelle in its speed (ch. 23:22), and God gave it strength to triumph over all the nations that oppress it and destroy them, and "break their arrows," meaning "Agag," that is, take away from its enemies their strength and their honor.

24.6.1.en: He lay down: he sat and settled on the ground.

24.6.2.en: This people sat in its place in a state of alertness and readiness to leap and seize its enemies, like the lion and the lioness, which no one can move, and everyone who blesses this people and does good to it, God blesses him, and everyone who curses this people or stands before it, God curses him.

24.6.3.en: This verse also signifies Christ, who rested on the Cross and by His death bound Satan and all his soldiers, for He is the Lion that came out of the tribe of Judah to save those who believe in Him.

24.7.0.en: Balaam ended his discourse and his third parable, and the result and Balak's reaction was rage and anger at Balaam, so he smote his hands together in astonishment and declared his distress, saying, I brought you and honored your hospitality to curse and revile my enemies, that is, the people of Israel, and behold, instead you have blessed them three times.

24.8.0.en: Also in anger Balak commanded Balaam to leave his land at once, "flee," and added that he had wanted to honor him if he cursed this people, but by these words of his he would receive no honor, for the Lord, Balaam's God, had kept him back from this honor.

24.9.0.en: Balaam defends himself by saying that he deceived no one, and clarified his earlier position, that he had promised nothing, and he reminds Balak of what he had told his messengers from the first, that he would not utter anything other than what God declares to him even if the enticement were all Balak's wealth). (ch. 23:18).

24.10.0.en: Balaam announces the end of his journey and mission and his return to his people, but he adds, addressing Balak, that before his going he will declare a last prophecy of what the people of the children of Israel will do to his people, and of course Balaam did not declare anything of his own but what the Lord declared to him also, and this prophecy was Balaam's fourth discourse, as we shall see.

24.10.1.en: If God is with you He blesses you, and the whole world cannot stand before you. So do not be shaken however much those who wrong you increase, for God protects you from their rage and their threats and establishes your peace.

24.11.0.en: Balaam began his fourth discourse with what he had said at the beginning of his third discourse in (vv. 3, 4).

24.12.0.en: The corners of Moab: that is, its strength, because a people fortifies its borders with its military strength, and what is meant is the breaking of its strength.

24.12.1.en: Tumult (sons of Sheth): war, and what is meant is the destruction of everyone who fights him.

24.12.2.en: Balaam began his fourth discourse with a speech that may seem obscure, for he speaks of some person and not of the people of Israel, and describes this person as follows:

24.12.3.en: 1- He is a man, but the time of his coming is not the present time but he will come in the distant future.

24.12.4.en: 2- He will be a star in his brightness and shining, a clear indication of his purity and righteousness.

24.12.5.en: 3- He carries a scepter in his hands, for he is a king and has absolute authority and sovereignty.

24.12.6.en: 4- He smites the corners of Moab, that is, by his coming he declares the end of the pagan worships, which Moab symbolizes.

24.12.7.en: 5- He destroys the sons of tumult: that is, he rules over and destroys the wicked by the authority of his everlasting kingdom.

24.12.8.en: It is clear that all the speech here has no relation to Balak and the people of Israel, but the divine inspiration used Balaam to utter a prophecy that applies to none of mankind except the Lord Christ, God incarnate, who alone has authority, kingship and glory. And Christ is the One who will come from the people of the children of Israel and break the power of the wicked, which Moab symbolizes.

24.13.0.en: Edom: they are the descendants of Esau.

24.13.1.en: Seir: the mountains of Seir are the regions in which the Edomites lived.

24.13.2.en: And among the attributes of Christ also is that He reigns over the neighboring peoples and subdues them to Himself, so the Gentiles believe in Him and He reigns over the hearts of those who are symbolized by the people of Edom, that is, Christianity spreads among the Gentiles.

24.14.0.en: And the authority of Christ will be over every city, that is, the whole world, but those who did not accept Him as King over them, that is, the wanderers, their end is destruction.

24.15.0.en: Amalek: they are the descendants of Eliphaz, firstborn of Esau (Gen 36:13, 14), and their land was south of Canaan.

24.15.1.en: Balaam saw another sight in his vision and declared it concerning the people of Amalek, who always represented the wicked peoples that resisted the people of God (Ex 17:8), so he says that Amalek was the first of the nations to fight the people of God and resist it and was also the strongest of the peoples at this time, but look at his end, for God destroyed him; God may permit the wicked to exist for a while or for some time, but their end is always destruction.

24.16.0.en: The Kenite: they are the descendants of a man called "Cain" who lived in the regions where the Edomites lived.

24.16.1.en: Thy dwellingplace ... thy nest: the place of your residence.

24.16.2.en: These two verses point to some tribes who lived in the mountains and caves, descended from Cain, and who thought that they were immune from evil and destruction, but the time of the Assyrian state will come and it will take possession, that is, take captive, these tribes.

24.17.0.en: Balaam completes his speech and says, but who shall live and survive until all these future events happen? No one of the present generation, and what is meant is that this prophecy relates to the relatively distant future.

24.18.0.en: Chittim: a name that was given to the island of Cyprus and was also given to the European kingdoms, which include the Greek and Roman kingdoms.

24.18.1.en: Ships will come from beyond the sea, whether carrying the Greeks led by Alexander the Great first and then followed by the Romans second, and these new nations will subdue the kingdoms before them such as Babylon and Assyria, and also Eber, that is, the Jewish kingdom, who are the Hebrews, the descendants of Eber, and the whole region of the East and the Mediterranean basin. And he also shall perish for ever: what is meant here is the new invader, that is, the Greeks and the Romans, for even the new powerful kingdoms, with all their philosophy or power, will not stand before the great Star that comes out of Jacob, that is, Christ (v. 17). With these messianic prophecies concerning Christ Balaam ended his fourth and last discourse.

24.19.0.en: The end of the meeting was in parting, so Balaam and Balak each went to the way of his return and the place from which he had come.

24.19.1.en: The kingdoms of the world fluctuate and all its powers change, so do not be troubled by them or attached to them, but stand firm in your faith in Christ, who protects you in this world and gives you to enjoy bliss forever.

24.19.2.en: The fornication of Israel and the zeal of Phinehas
